46-021.r: Rani Lakshmibai's last battle → against Hugh Rose; died 18 June 1858 after leaving Jhansi for Gwalior. Rose called her the only man among the rebels.
46-021.t: Havelock and Neil fought at Lucknow, not against the Rani.

46-022.r: 1857 at Lucknow (Oudh) → Begum Hazrat Mahal, from 30 May 1857; crowned minor son Birjis Qadr; Colin Campbell retook Lucknow on 21 March 1858 with Gorkhas.

46-025.r: Leader of 1857 at Allahabad (Prayagraj) → Maulvi Liyaqat Ali, religious teacher from village Mahgaon, Chail pargana.

46-026.r: Largest number of 1857 sepoys came from Oudh → over 75,000; one member from each family joined.

46-027.r: Nana Saheb's commander-in-chief → Tatya Tope; Nana was proclaimed Peshwa at Kanpur on 5 June 1857.

46-028.r: Azimullah Khan → adviser and secretary of Nana Saheb; called "Krantidoot".

46-029.r: 1857 leader betrayed by a friend, captured and executed → Tatya Tope (real name Ramchandra Pandurang Tope), follower of Nana Saheb; defeated by Napier's troops.

46-031.r: Kunwar Singh → Bihar; born at Jagdishpur (Shahabad), led the revolt at Arrah though nearly eighty years old.

46-033.r: Kunwar Singh joined the 1857 revolt at Arrah; he led the revolt in Bihar.
46-033.t: BPSC's key said Patna; the book calls that wrong - Arrah is right.

46-041.r: True: Syed Ahmad Khan wrote Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind ('Causes of the Indian Revolt'); Hazrat Mahal led Lucknow. False: Mangal Pandey hanged 8 April 1857, not 29 March; Nana Saheb not at Bareilly.
46-041.c: Answer not printed; explanation makes only 1 and 3 true, which matches no option.

46-042.r: Only 1: Kunwar Singh, zamindar of Jagdishpur (Bihar), led the revolt. Dalhousie refused to accept Lakshmibai's adopted son Damodar after Gangadhar Rao died (1853).

46-043.r: 1857 at Patna (Danapur) → old zamindar Kunwar Singh, who had lost his zamindari through British policies.

46-044.r: 1857 in Assam → Diwan Maniram Dutta; planned to crown Kandarpeshwar Singh (last king's grandson); hanged by the British.

46-045.r: Centre of 1857 revolt in Bihar (15 July 1857 - 20 January 1858) → Jagdishpur, where Kunwar Singh ran his own government; crushed by William Taylor and Major Vincent Eyre.

46-046.r: Defeated the joint British-Jodhpur army in 1857 → Thakur Kushal Singh of Auwa (Rajasthan).

46-047.r: Not a centre of 1857 → Jaipur; Ajmer, Neemuch and Auwa were centres.

46-048.r: Fought the British in 1857 → Saadat (Ali) Khan, at Indore; Azad, Bismil and Makhan Lal Chaturvedi belong to later times.

46-049.r: Bitterest enemy of the British in 1857 → Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah, leader at Faizabad (Ayodhya), originally from Chinapattan (Madras); called "best soldier among the rebels".

46-050.r: Bhopal's hero of 1857 who led the movement and died → Nawab Fazil Mohammad Khan.

46-051.r: Poet who witnessed the Revolt of 1857 → Mirza Ghalib.

46-052.r: Mirza Ghalib → born in Agra (27 Dec 1797), died in Delhi (15 Feb 1869).
46-052.t: Original home Agra, not Delhi where he lived and died.

46-053.r: Not linked to 1857 → Bhagat Singh; Tatya Tope, Rani Lakshmibai and Bahadur Shah Zafar were rebel leaders.

46-054.r: Not linked to 1857 → Uddham Singh (later Punjab revolutionary). Kunwar Singh → Arrah; Begum Hazrat Mahal → Lucknow; Maulavi Ahmadullah → Faizabad.

46-055.r: Biggest supporters of the British in 1857 → Scindias of Gwalior (also Nizam, Holkars); Canning: "If Scindia joins the rebels, I will pack off tomorrow."

46-056.r: Educated middle class in 1857 → stayed neutral, hoping the British would bring progress; a major reason the revolt failed.

46-057.r: Groups that did not join 1857 → Sahukars (moneylenders) and Landlords; rulers of Patiala, Jind, Gwalior, Hyderabad helped the British.

46-058.r: Did not rebel against Company control → Nizam of Hyderabad; Raja of Vijayanagaram, Polygars of Tamil Nadu and Diwan Velu Thampi of Travancore did.

46-059.r: Not affected by 1857 → Chittor. Centres: Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Jagdishpur (Kunwar Singh), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal).

46-060.r: Part of Bihar unaffected in 1857 → Munger; centres were Arrah, Danapur, Gaya, Patna, Muzaffarpur, Shahabad.

46-061.r: Bakht Khan → Delhi; Maulvi Ahmadullah → Awadh; Kunwar Singh → Arrah; Nana Saheb → Kanpur.

46-062.r: Kunwar Singh → Jagdishpur; Hazrat Mahal → Lucknow; Khan Bahadur Khan → Bareilly; Maulvi Ahmadullah → Faizabad.

46-063.r: Jhansi → Rani Laxmibai; Lucknow → Begum Hazrat Mahal; Kanpur → Azimullah Khan; Faizabad → Maulvi Ahmad(ullah) Shah.

46-064.r: Wrong pair: Lucknow - Liyaqat Ali → he led at Allahabad. Correct: Sambalpur - Surendra Sai; Ganjam - Radhakrishna Dandsena; Kashmir - Gulab Singh.

46-065.r: Active 1857 leaders → Nana Saheb (Kanpur), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Maulavi Ahmadullah (Faizabad); more than one option is right.

46-066.r: Nana Saheb → Kanpur; Nawab Hamid Ali Khan → Delhi; Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah → Lucknow; Maniram Diwan → Assam.

46-067.r: Wrong pair: Jhansi - 11 May 1857 → Jhansi rose 4 June 1857. Correct: Barrackpore 29 March; Meerut 10 May (3rd Bengal Light Cavalry); Lucknow 30 May/4 June.

46-068.r: Governor-General during the 1857 revolt → Lord Canning, last Company GG and first Crown Viceroy; Widow Remarriage Act 1856, High Courts Act 1861 (Bombay, Calcutta, Madras).

46-072.r: British commanding officer at Barrackpore in 1857 → Lt Gen Sir John Bennet Hearsey.

46-073.r: Allahabad (Prayagraj) made emergency headquarters in 1857 → Lord Canning.

46-074.r: British Prime Minister during the 1857 revolt → Viscount Palmerston (1855-1858, again 1859-1865).

46-075.r: Col. St. Leger, Lt. Col. Gibbs and Col. Wallace → none of them linked to the Revolt of 1857 (all of the above).

46-076.r: Main cause of 1857's failure → no common strategy or central leadership; groups fought for their own interests, with no nationalism or clear vision.

46-077.r: 1857 failed → all: no unity of purpose, native kings backed the British, better-armed British; also limited spread, troops back from Crimea, no Sikh or educated-class support.

46-080.r: Died at Lucknow → Sir Henry Lawrence, Havelock, Neil (2, 3, 4); John Nicholson died at Delhi (Sept 1857) during its recapture.

46-081.r: 1857 failed because Bahadur Shah Zafar's leadership lacked wide support and major Indian rulers stayed away or backed the British (A and R true, R explains A).

46-082.r: Called 1857 a conspiracy → Sir James Outram and W. Taylor (Hindu-Muslim plot); Seeley → 'Sepoy Mutiny'; T.R. Holmes → civilisation vs barbarism.

46-083.r: Called 1857 the 'First War of Independence' → V.D. Savarkar, in 'The Indian War of Independence 1857' (a well-planned revolt).
hi: First War of Independence (प्रथम स्वतंत्रता संग्राम)

46-087.r: Official historian of the Indian freedom struggle (the Revolt) → S.N. Sen, author of 'Eighteen Fifty-seven', published 1957.
46-087.h: Sen's book came out a hundred years after the revolt it describes.

46-088.r: First Indian to write in an Indian language on causes of 1857 → Syed Ahmad Khan, 'Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind' (written 1858, published 1859).

46-089.r: "Neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence" → R.C. Majumdar, in 'The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857'.
46-089.t: Savarkar praised it as First War of Independence; Majumdar rejected that label.

46-091.r: Historian who refused to call 1857 a national war of independence → R.C. Majumdar; he left the government project and wrote his own book.

46-092.r: 'Indian nationalism was embryonic in the mid-19th century' → view of R.C. Majumdar and S.N. Sen.

46-093.r: 1857 gave a death blow to East India Company rule; Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 Nov 1858) put India under the Crown.

46-095.r: Promise of Queen's Proclamation (1 Nov 1858) actually kept → policy of annexation abandoned; read by Lord Canning at the Allahabad Durbar.

46-096.r: Queen's Proclamation / Act of 1858 → disclaimed annexing Indian States and placed India under the Crown (1 and 2); not to regulate Company trade.

46-097.r: Army reorganisation after the 1857 revolt → Peel Commission.

46-098.r: After 1857 the British recruited Gurkhas, Sikhs and Punjabis of the North, distrusting U.P. and Bihar sepoys (60% of Bengal Army had been from Oudh and North West Provinces).

47-001.r: Bengal upheaval just after 1857 → Indigo Revolt (1859-60), began at Govindpur, Nadia, led by Digambar and Bishnu Biswas; 'Neel Darpan' by Dinabandhu Mitra.
47-001.t: Sanyasi 1763-1800, Santhal 1855-56 and Pabna 1873-76 are not right after 1857.

47-007.r: Order: Sanyasi Rebellion (1763-1800) → Indigo Revolt (1859-60) → Kuka Rebellion (1871-72) → Pabna movement (1873-76).

47-008.r: Indigo cultivation declined by the early 20th century → it became unprofitable in the world market because of new artificial dyes.
